question: Can the neural networks used by supervised learning, learning by confusion, and parameter regression for phase-transition detection be replaced by closed-form Bayes-optimal predictors, and what do those predictors reveal about when the resulting indicators succeed or fail?

key_findings.claim: The supervised-learning optimum is the posterior probability that an input came from the first labeled parameter region rather than the second.
key_findings.evidence: For an input x present in the training support, minimizing binary cross-entropy gives P_I(x)/(P_I(x)+P_II(x)), where P_I and P_II sum the parameter-conditioned input probabilities over the two labeled boundary regions. Averaging this posterior under each P_k and taking a negative parameter derivative produces the proposed supervised indicator. This is the standard Bayes classifier for the imposed region labels, expressed in the paper's phase-scan notation.

key_findings.claim: Learning by confusion reduces to a Bayes classifier for every candidate bipartition, so its optimal score measures probability-distribution overlap rather than an order parameter.
key_findings.evidence: For each of K+1 splits, the optimal prediction is again P_I(x)/(P_I(x)+P_II(x)). The optimal accuracy is one minus the average smaller posterior mass, so a peak marks the split with least class overlap. The result explains the W/V-shaped baselines and also why perfect sample distinguishability can erase an informative interior maximum.

key_findings.claim: The prediction-based-method optimum is the conditional mean of the scan parameter given an input.
key_findings.evidence: Minimizing mean squared error gives sum_k P_k(x)p_k divided by sum_k P_k(x). Its averaged prediction and the derivative of prediction error form the PBM indicator. This is an ordinary Bayes regressor: a peak can occur where conditional parameter identifiability changes, but the loss does not directly optimize phase-boundary accuracy.

key_findings.claim: The word 'optimal' applies to the surrogate cross-entropy or squared-error task, not to critical-point detection.
key_findings.evidence: The paper itself supplies counterexamples where the globally loss-minimizing predictor yields a worse physical indicator than a restricted, underfit neural network. The post-hoc derivative or accuracy indicator is not part of the optimized objective. Thus Bayes optimality for labels or parameter regression does not imply statistical optimality, consistency, or minimax efficiency for locating a phase transition.

key_findings.claim: The three prototypical examples correctly expose the dependence on distribution overlap and are closely matched by sufficiently trained neural networks.
key_findings.evidence: Identical distributions yield a flat supervised indicator, a V-shaped confusion score, and PBM indicator -1. A clean two-region distribution yields sharp transition signals. Mutually disjoint parameter-conditioned supports instead give perfect confusion accuracy and exact parameter regression, causing LBC and PBM to report no informative boundary despite the constructed discontinuity. Figure 2 shows the analytical and neural curves nearly coinciding.

key_findings.claim: The Ising experiment directly demonstrates that a more accurate surrogate predictor can be a worse transition detector.
key_findings.evidence: For the L=60 Ising model, optimal supervised learning tracks the probability of the ground-state energy and its peak drifts toward zero temperature with increasing L. Optimal PBM develops a dominant spurious low-temperature peak plus a smaller critical peak. LBC locates the critical temperature. Small, early-stopped, or regularized neural networks recover the desired Ising peak precisely because they do not minimize the surrogate loss as well as the analytical predictor.

key_findings.claim: The Ising-gauge-theory example shows a different failure pattern: the high-capacity SL and PBM optima are useful while LBC is intrinsically ambiguous.
key_findings.evidence: The finite-size topological crossover is detected by the optimal SL scaling and the dominant PBM peak, whereas the optimal LBC curve has the distorted ambiguity previously seen with neural networks. Reducing capacity makes SL/PBM track the heat-capacity peak, which does not mark the stated crossover. This prevents a universal prescription that either exact Bayes optimization or underfitting is always preferable.

anchors.section: IV.B / LBC ambiguity and capacity discussion

key_findings.claim: All three optimal objectives miss the XY model's BKT transition accurately in the reported large-system regime.
key_findings.evidence: Optimal SL again emphasizes disappearance of the ground state; LBC peaks near the heat-capacity maximum around kBT/J=1 rather than the cited BKT value 0.8935; PBM's finite-size peak fades as the distributions become more distinguishable. The helicity-modulus crossing independently matches the literature value. Restricted models can create a near-critical peak, but that is an inductive-bias effect rather than validation of the Bayes optimum.

key_findings.claim: The quantum examples support narrow finite-size, representation-specific success rather than general quantum scaling.
key_findings.evidence: SL, LBC, and PBM locate the selected XXZ transition for chains through L=14, the Kitaev transition for chains through L=20, and a broad Bose-Hubbard many-body-localization reference region using L=6/8. The inputs are probabilities of outcomes in chosen Sz or Fock bases, often from exact diagonalization. No thermodynamic extrapolation, basis sweep for every system, experimental noise model, or resource scaling beyond these small sizes is reported.

key_findings.claim: Finite sampling can reverse the meaning of the exact indicator because empirical supports become artificially disjoint.
key_findings.evidence: For the L=20 Kitaev chain with 524,288 basis states, SL and PBM obtain useful locations around 10^3 samples per scan point, while LBC needs about 10^4 before an interior local maximum appears. At lower M, LBC approaches perfect accuracy and PBM nearly reproduces p because each sample identifies its scan point, even though the exact distributions overlap. The authors average 100 synthetic data sets for this appendix experiment.

key_findings.claim: The neural-network reachability experiments show approximation of the analytical curves only after substantial, system-specific tuning.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 11-12 use 300-10,000 epochs, architectures ranging from three 64-unit layers to five layers with 128/64 units, and hand-selected tasks and system sizes. The curves are visually close for the smallest reported systems, but no numerical approximation error, convergence probability over seeds, matched hyperparameter budget, or held-out metric is supplied. The claim that sufficiently large well-trained networks recover the optima is therefore qualitatively illustrated rather than quantitatively benchmarked.

key_findings.claim: The runtime comparison is a component benchmark, not an end-to-end speedup measurement.
key_findings.evidence: Table I compares construction and evaluation of the analytical predictor with one epoch of a one-hidden-node neural network on one CPU. It explicitly excludes sample generation and probability-distribution construction, while useful neural results use hundreds to thousands of epochs. LBC remains O(Mbar K^2), takes 32.0+/-1.7 seconds on the L=20 Kitaev case, and is 204-1231 times slower than analytical SL across the table. These measurements support avoiding iterative fitting once a discrete distribution table exists, but not a universal advantage on raw high-dimensional data.

key_findings.claim: The exact arXiv source is substantially inspectable and rebuildable, but its standard bibliography path is broken.
key_findings.evidence: The v2 e-print has SHA256 361ed7487a3759bfab01de0afb8e6272a1943826812cf72f45d533869fa14e8f and contains the TeX, bibliography, rendered bibliography, and all 20 PNG figures, but no numerical code or raw results. Two direct pdflatex passes using the bundled main.bbl rebuild 39 pages. A normal latexmk/BibTeX rebuild fails because refs.bib contains an empty `number = ,` field; the source also defines `eq:app_b11` twice. All 20 figures and Table I were visually audited.

anchors.section: Open-source statement and Appendix A start

key_findings.claim: The official code artifact reproduces only a minority of the paper's physical-system workflows.
key_findings.evidence: The official repository's current HEAD is 8045f5fc1de45434e4efaf818f05e37bf38f8ac6; the v2-era code commit is 03078c4db1ed224dbf6ac96f259fbc95d011e168, and the Julia source is unchanged between them. The repository supplies examples/data for the prototypes, Ising, and L=6/8 MBL Bose-Hubbard cases, but not executable IGT, XY, XXZ, Kitaev, Gutzwiller, figure-generation, timing-table, or finite-size pipelines. It has no raw result arrays, checkpoints, tests, CI, tag, or release.

key_findings.claim: The supervised-loss normalization is off by one in both the explanatory equation and released code.
key_findings.evidence: Page 7 defines K_II=K-l_II even though region II contains sampled points l_II through K and therefore has K-l_II+1 points. For the paper's common r_I=1,l_II=K setup, the printed definition makes K_II zero while Figure 2 and the correct posterior require one point in each region. The official Julia functions divide by p_min_indx+K-p_max_indx, repeating the missing +1 and scaling both analytical and neural supervised loss values. Predictions and derivative indicators are not changed by this constant loss scaling, but reported loss comparisons and stopping values are.

key_findings.claim: The released finite-sample pseudocount routine does not implement the normalized distribution described in the paper.
key_findings.evidence: Page 26 says every unseen boundary input is added once and the boundary distribution becomes count/(M+M_notinT). The code instead inserts 1/M into each zero row and never renormalizes existing probabilities. On the released Ising data, the L=10 last-column mass becomes 1.00028 (28 unseen of 100,000) and the L=60 mass becomes 1.01539 (1,539 unseen), rather than one. This affects neural supervised training and standardization in the supplied examples, although it does not alter the main analytical curves computed from the unmodified tables.

key_findings.claim: The non-default threaded supervised implementation has a shared-state data race.
key_findings.evidence: The official function `get_indicators_SL_analytical_threaded` mutates the same scalar `loss` with `loss +=` inside two `Threads.@threads` loops without an atomic operation or reduction. Concurrent writes can be lost, making the returned analytical loss nondeterministic and too small. The prediction and indicator arrays use disjoint indices and are not affected by this particular race.

key_findings.claim: All three released neural training loops can return zero or mismatched 'best' parameters.
key_findings.evidence: At epoch one, each loop records the loss but does not copy the initialized or updated parameters into `pnn_best`; a one-epoch run, or any run with no later strict improvement, logs the all-zero parameter vector. On a later improvement, it compares the pre-update loss but copies parameters after the update, so the saved parameters do not correspond to the loss that selected them. The same pattern appears in SL, LBC, and PBM and can corrupt early-stopping or saved-best outputs.

key_findings.claim: The released LBC evaluation path computes the wrong loss when asked to recalculate it.
key_findings.evidence: In `predict_LBC(calc_loss=true)`, operator precedence divides only the second class-region cross-entropy sum by K; the first sum is left unnormalized before regularization is added. This disagrees with both Equation 4 and the repository's own `main_loss_LBC`, and is the path used when a supplied trained parameter vector is evaluated. Classification accuracy is calculated separately and is unaffected.

anchors.section: Appendix B / LBC training and loss reporting

key_findings.claim: The cross-entropy derivation is not literally valid at the boundary optima that dominate several examples.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix obtains the posterior by setting an interior derivative to zero and then asserts a strictly positive second derivative. When an input appears in only one class region, the optimum is exactly zero or one; the printed derivative and Hessian contain logarithmic or reciprocal boundary terms and are not defined as written. The posterior formula is still recoverable from convex conditional-risk minimization with boundary limits, so this is a proof-presentation defect rather than a refutation of the formula.

key_findings.claim: The Boltzmann PBM loss derivation uses a false label identity.
key_findings.evidence: Pages 24-25 rewrite the regression label as y(x)=y(H(x)). In PBM the label is the externally chosen scan parameter p_k, and the same energy can occur at multiple temperatures, so energy does not determine the label. The intended grouping remains repairable by retaining y_k=p_k inside each k-indexed sum; the printed functional identity is false and the duplicate equation label in the source compounds the ambiguity.

key_findings.claim: The claimed representation generality is conditional and can fail under information-losing or symmetry-breaking encodings.
key_findings.evidence: The paper correctly notes that a change of quantum measurement basis changes the observed distributions and can move the inferred transition, then later says multiple representations give the same optimum only if they preserve the relevant distributions. Using energy rather than raw spin configurations explicitly injects Hamiltonian knowledge and collapses an exponentially large state space. Later representation-dependent studies confirm that raw and symmetry-respecting encodings can make the same unsupervised method fail or succeed.

key_findings.claim: The released neural results lack deterministic seed and repetition support.
key_findings.evidence: The paper gives error bars for selected finite-data experiments and extensive pointwise curves, but the repository contains no Random.seed! call, seed list, test suite, CI, or repeated-run driver for the main neural figures. Neural initialization and optimization are therefore not reproducible bit-for-bit, and the reachability figures expose no seed count or uncertainty. The pinned Manifest targets Julia 1.7.2 and Flux 0.12.9, but no tagged paper release exists.

anchors.section: Appendix B / neural architecture and training

key_findings.claim: The classical Monte Carlo protocol leaves correlation, initialization, and uncertainty questions unresolved.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix reports 10^5 thermalization sweeps and 10^5 collected samples, with temperatures increased sequentially for Ising/IGT and decreased for XY. It does not state thinning, integrated autocorrelation times, independent-chain counts, hysteresis checks, effective sample sizes, or uncertainty on most phase estimates. Energy histogram binning is tuned until visual convergence, while derivative indicators can amplify residual binning and Monte Carlo noise.

anchors.section: Appendix A.5 / Monte Carlo versus enumeration

key_findings.claim: The paper correctly rejects V-shaped background subtraction as a generic LBC repair.
key_findings.evidence: Subtracting the indistinguishable-data baseline biases the largest peak toward the center of the scan window. Figure 20 shows the shift across Ising, IGT, XY, XXZ, Kitaev, and Bose-Hubbard examples. This is a useful negative result: cosmetic removal of the trivial confusion shape can change the estimator rather than isolate a physical signal.

key_findings.claim: The additional Gutzwiller Bose-Hubbard example supplies an explicit representation-sensitive failure of LBC.
key_findings.evidence: Using Fock-basis indices from a product-state Gutzwiller calculation, SL and PBM mark the stated Mott-superfluid transition while optimal LBC fails. The paper contrasts this with prior neural LBC using Gutzwiller coefficients directly. The example reinforces that the task and input representation, not merely classifier capacity, control success; it is also a mean-field calculation rather than a many-body benchmark.

key_findings.claim: Several visual and source defects are nonfatal but show that the published artifact was not mechanically checked end to end.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 10's caption refers to panels (d) and (f) while the rendered figure has panels a-e and no f; the text extraction and image reveal the PBM-indicator panel mislabeled in the caption. Figure 13 says 'vetical'; page 30 contains a rendered `/dieresis.ts1` artifact; page 4 defines the final LBC point as p1+Delta p/2 instead of pK+Delta p/2. These do not change the main curves but complicate exact figure-to-claim correspondence.

key_findings.claim: Later Fisher-information work gives the phase indicators a sharper target and exposes what this paper does not validate.
key_findings.evidence: A 2023 same-author successor relates several ML indicators to lower bounds on square-root Fisher information; ClassiFIM then defines FIM estimation with explicit error metrics and public ground truth; 2026 distance learning estimates f-divergences and critical exponents from snapshots. These works retain the useful distribution-change insight while adding an estimand, quantitative comparison, and finite-size analysis. They do not negate the closed-form formulas, but they narrow their role to diagnostics of three surrogate tasks.

method.core_idea: Replace each trained neural predictor by the exact conditional-risk minimizer induced by empirical parameter-conditioned input distributions, then feed that predictor through the original phase-indicator post-processing.
method.mechanism: For supervised learning and each learning-by-confusion split, compute a posterior from summed class-region probability masses. For PBM, compute the conditional mean of the scan parameter. Average predictions under every scan-point distribution and use central finite differences or splitwise accuracy to obtain indicators. Estimate the distributions by frequency tables, sometimes after a physics-informed representation such as energy or a measurement-basis index, and compare the analytical curves with trained neural networks and physical reference observables.
assumptions: The scan grid and its sampling weights define the class priors; the formulas use effectively uniform weighting across sampled parameter values.
Samples are drawn independently from stable parameter-conditioned distributions, or empirical frequencies are adequate approximations despite Monte Carlo correlation.
The chosen representation preserves the probability-distribution change relevant to the transition.
For supervised learning, evaluation inputs are covered by the labeled boundary-region training support or an explicit unseen-input convention is supplied.
The desired phase boundary coincides with a prominent extremum of the post-hoc derivative or classification-accuracy indicator.
At most two adjacent phases need to be separated in one scan, with multiphase diagrams handled piecewise.
A sufficiently expressive neural network and optimizer can reach the global conditional-risk optimum when neural reachability is claimed.
Finite grid spacing, density estimation, and numerical differentiation are fine enough for peak locations to be meaningful.
For quantum data, the selected measurement basis or classical representation contains enough phase information.
Construction and storage of the empirical probability table are computationally feasible.

techniques.role: Computes the exact cross-entropy minimizer for supervised and confusion labels from class-region probability masses.
Computes the exact squared-error PBM prediction as the parameter mean conditioned on an observed input.
Interprets confusion accuracy and prediction error through overlap among parameter-conditioned distributions.
Replaces neural fitting with frequency counts over unique inputs, energies, or basis states.
Transforms averaged supervised or regression predictions into a phase-scan signal on interior grid points.
Evaluates K+1 candidate left-right labelings for learning by confusion.
Uses energy or measurement-basis indices to reduce the input state space and improve empirical density estimates.
Uses width, training duration, and L2 regularization to interpolate between simple inductive bias and the Bayes surrogate optimum.
Measures how sparse empirical support changes indicator behavior relative to exact distributions.
Tracks peak locations with lattice or chain size and compares them with physical reference observables.

evaluations.setting: Three prototypical distribution families on a one-dimensional parameter grid
evaluations.metric: Agreement of analytical and neural predictions, losses, and phase indicators
evaluations.result: The trained neural curves closely match the closed-form optima; mutually disjoint supports reveal that LBC and PBM can lose the constructed boundary signal despite perfect surrogate performance.
evaluations.baseline: Neural SL, LBC, and PBM trained for the same synthetic tasks.

evaluations.setting: Two-dimensional Ising model, up to L=60
evaluations.metric: Peak location and finite-size behavior relative to exact critical temperature
evaluations.result: Optimal LBC locates the transition; optimal SL drifts toward zero temperature and optimal PBM has a dominant spurious low-temperature peak. Restricted neural PBM/SL can locate the physical transition better than their exact surrogate optima.
evaluations.baseline: Exact Ising critical temperature, heat capacity, magnetization, and prior neural implementations.

evaluations.setting: Wegner Ising gauge theory, up to L=28
evaluations.result: Optimal SL and the dominant PBM peak track the finite-size crossover; LBC is ambiguous at larger sizes, while lower-capacity models can move SL/PBM toward the wrong heat-capacity feature.
evaluations.baseline: First violated plaquette constraint, stated crossover scaling, and heat capacity.

evaluations.setting: Two-dimensional XY model, up to L=60
evaluations.result: Optimal SL fails, LBC follows the heat-capacity maximum above Tc, and PBM loses its finite-size peak; the helicity-modulus crossing matches the cited 0.8935 reference.
evaluations.baseline: Literature BKT value, helicity modulus, heat capacity, and magnetization.

evaluations.setting: XXZ and Kitaev chains, up to L=14 and L=20
evaluations.metric: Peak convergence to known quantum critical points
evaluations.result: All three analytical indicators approach Delta/J=-1 for the selected XXZ boundary and mu/t=-2 for the Kitaev boundary in the chosen measurement bases.
evaluations.baseline: Magnetization, reduced-density-matrix eigenvalue derivative, and entanglement entropy.

evaluations.setting: Quasiperiodic one-dimensional Bose-Hubbard MBL dynamics, L=6/8
evaluations.metric: Location relative to W/J approximately 4-7 and spectral-statistics crossover
evaluations.result: All three indicators change in the broad reference interval and near the retrieval-probability rise; no thermodynamic critical extrapolation is performed.
evaluations.baseline: Consecutive-level-spacing ratios and prior numerical/experimental analysis.

evaluations.setting: Finite-sample Kitaev measurement distributions, L=20 and 524,288 basis states
evaluations.metric: Samples per parameter value required for an informative peak
evaluations.result: SL/PBM give useful locations near 10^3 samples, while LBC needs roughly 10^4; 100 independent sampled data sets quantify dispersion.

evaluations.setting: Neural approximation across six physical systems
evaluations.metric: Visual agreement with analytical predictions and indicators
evaluations.result: System-specific networks trained for 300-10,000 epochs qualitatively recover the analytical curves on selected small systems, without a numerical curve-error metric or multi-seed success rate.
evaluations.baseline: Closed-form analytical curves and optimal loss.

evaluations.setting: Single-CPU component timing on six systems
evaluations.metric: Seconds for analytical construction/evaluation versus one epoch of a one-node network
evaluations.result: Analytical SL/PBM take under one second; analytical LBC reaches 32.0+/-1.7 seconds and costs 204-1231 times analytical SL. Neural PBM/LBC single epochs are mostly 1.3-4.2 times slower, but data construction and full training are excluded.
evaluations.baseline: One epoch of an intentionally minimal neural network, not a converged end-to-end pipeline.

evaluations.metric: Whether each indicator marks the stated Mott-superfluid point
evaluations.result: SL and PBM succeed with Fock-index inputs; LBC fails, unlike prior LBC using Gutzwiller coefficients directly.
evaluations.baseline: Mean occupation, energy, and the mean-field critical reference.

evaluations.setting: Exact arXiv source and all 20 figures plus Table I
evaluations.result: Every extracted page and visual was audited; bundled-bbl pdflatex rebuild succeeds to 39 pages, while standard BibTeX fails on malformed refs.bib and the source has a duplicate equation label.
evaluations.baseline: A clean one-command source rebuild with unambiguous figure-panel correspondence.

evaluations.result: Only prototypes, Ising, and MBL examples are present; static audit finds a threaded race, three checkpoint bugs, an LBC loss bug, off-by-one normalization, and a non-normalized pseudocount path. No tests or CI are present.
evaluations.baseline: A tagged, seeded, tested artifact reproducing all six systems, appendices, figures, and timing tables.

limitations: Bayes optimality is proved for surrogate classification or regression losses, not for the phase-boundary estimator created afterward.
The indicators can fail even with exact distributions; the paper's Ising, XY, and Gutzwiller examples explicitly show this.
Success depends on the scan range, grid, labels, representation, and quantum measurement basis.
Empirical density estimation can require storage and sampling exponential in system size; energy compression injects Hamiltonian knowledge.
Sparse support can make parameter values perfectly distinguishable and erase useful LBC/PBM signals.
Central differences omit endpoints and amplify sampling or histogram noise; no general smoothing or uncertainty rule is supplied.
The neural reachability study is visually judged, hand-tuned, and lacks seeds, approximation metrics, and success probabilities.
Runtime measurements exclude sample generation and density-table construction and compare with only one epoch of a one-node network.
The quantum studies are limited to small exact-diagonalization systems and one chosen representation per headline result.
The MBL reference is a broad finite-size interval, not a sharply validated thermodynamic critical point.
The classical Monte Carlo protocol does not report autocorrelation, thinning, effective sample size, or hysteresis checks.
The official artifact covers only part of the paper and has no tests, CI, seeds, tags, releases, raw outputs, or result-generation scripts.
Several official Julia paths return incorrectly normalized losses or distributions and can save the wrong neural parameters.
The cross-entropy proof needs boundary-limit handling when exact posteriors are zero or one.
Piecewise handling of more than two phases requires external scan decomposition and can miss multicritical structure.
Peak selection still needs finite-size scaling or physical analysis to distinguish transitions, crossovers, and spurious distribution changes.
failure_modes: Ground-state probability changes dominate an SL/PBM derivative far from the actual critical point.
A heat-capacity or other crossover feature produces the largest distribution change while the desired topological transition is subtler.
A high-dimensional empirical support is nearly duplicate-free, giving perfect classification/regression and no interior transition signal.
A many-to-one representation removes the order or correlation needed to distinguish phases.
A symmetry-breaking raw representation separates physically equivalent states and creates artificial clusters or overlap patterns.
A small change to scan endpoints moves a global peak or changes the LBC center bias.
Finite-difference noise produces a false maximum, especially for SL and PBM.
Underfit models accidentally locate one benchmark transition but fail on another, as capacity effects reverse between Ising and IGT.
Unseen supervised inputs make the Bayes prediction undefined; zeroing, pseudocounting, and interpolation yield different indicators.
Sequential Monte Carlo temperature scans retain hysteresis or correlated samples that distort empirical probabilities.
Threaded analytical SL loses updates to its shared loss accumulator.
One-epoch or never-improving neural runs return an all-zero best-parameter vector.
The trained=true LBC path reports a class-imbalanced, incorrectly normalized loss.
The released pseudocount path creates columns whose probability mass exceeds one.
LBC's O(Mbar K^2) computation becomes prohibitive for fine multidimensional phase diagrams.
reusable_insights: Derive the conditional-risk optimum before interpreting a neural model; it separates properties of the objective from optimizer or architecture artifacts.
A physically desirable underfit predictor signals objective mismatch, not necessarily successful regularization in general.
Distribution overlap is the central quantity behind confusion accuracy and parameter identifiability.
Evaluate phase indicators on exact toy distributions where supports are identical, cleanly separated, and disjoint before trusting them on physics data.
Separate representation cost and density-estimation cost from the cost of evaluating a closed-form predictor.
Report both surrogate loss and downstream critical-point error; improvements can move in opposite directions.
Treat measurement basis and symmetry-preserving preprocessing as part of the scientific method, not as neutral implementation details.
Sparse-support diagnostics should precede any claim that high classification accuracy reveals phases.
Use finite-size scaling and independent observables to distinguish phase transitions from crossovers and incidental distribution shifts.
Background subtraction can move an estimator; validate the transformed peak rather than assuming a prettier curve is more physical.
For empirical Bayes tables, explicitly specify unseen-event smoothing and verify every column remains normalized.
Test checkpoint invariants by checking that the saved parameters reproduce the loss that selected them.
Use reductions rather than shared scalar mutation in threaded scientific code.
Information-geometric quantities provide a more explicit target for comparing heterogeneous phase-detection indicators.
A full artifact should connect every figure to raw data, configuration, code revision, and deterministic regeneration command.
open_questions: Can one design a loss whose Bayes-optimal predictor is statistically consistent for a specified class of phase boundaries rather than merely for labels or p?
How do the three closed-form indicators relate exactly to Fisher information, total variation, Jensen-Shannon divergence, and other local distribution metrics?
What minimax sample complexity is required to locate a transition from high-dimensional snapshots under finite-size scaling?
Can density-ratio estimation compute the indicators without materializing an exponentially large empirical probability table?
Which smoothing rule for unseen supervised inputs preserves calibration and gives controlled critical-point bias?
Can uncertainty-aware derivatives replace central differences and return calibrated confidence intervals for peak locations?
How should multiple simultaneous phases, multicritical points, and first-order coexistence be handled without manual piecewise scans?
Can learned symmetry-invariant representations retain transition information without encoding the answer through a hand-selected observable such as energy?
How stable are the indicators across quantum measurement bases, shot noise, readout error, and incomplete observables?
Does an analytical predictor remain faster after including simulation, measurement, density estimation, memory, and hyperparameter selection end to end?
Can early stopping or capacity selection be chosen without knowing the critical point when the exact surrogate optimum is physically wrong?
What mechanism makes underfitting help Ising/XY but hurt the IGT example, and can that mechanism be predicted before training?
Can ClassiFIM-style ground-truth metrics fairly compare SL, LBC, PBM, generative classifiers, and distance learning on shared datasets?
Do the reported MBL signals persist under larger systems and modern finite-size analyses?
How much of the apparent distribution change is due to temperature-grid priors rather than intrinsic geometry of the physical family?
Can the official code be repaired and extended into a deterministic, tested package that regenerates all 20 figures and Table I?

competitive_landscape.title: Machine learning phases of matter
competitive_landscape.difference: Carrasquilla and Melko train neural classifiers on labeled endpoint phases and inspect their outputs; the target derives the exact Bayes posterior for that task and shows it can fail as a critical-point detector.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning phase transitions by confusion
competitive_landscape.difference: Van Nieuwenburg et al. propose scanning hypothetical label splits and looking for the W-shape; the target analytically reduces each split to posterior overlap and identifies intrinsic ambiguity cases.

competitive_landscape.title: Discovering Phase Transitions with Unsupervised Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang uses principal components to expose order and transitions without imposed phase labels; the target instead solves supervised/confusion/regression surrogate tasks exactly from empirical distributions.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised learning of phase transitions: from principal component analysis to variational autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: Wetzel compares PCA and variational autoencoders as similarity-based phase representations; the target avoids representation learning once a probability table has been chosen.

competitive_landscape.title: Discriminative Cooperative Networks for Detecting Phase Transitions
competitive_landscape.difference: Discriminative cooperative networks move candidate phase contours using classifier feedback in multidimensional diagrams; the target evaluates fixed one-dimensional split/posterior formulas and handles multiple phases only piecewise.

competitive_landscape.title: Quantum phase recognition via unsupervised machine learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Broecker et al. learn latent quantum-phase structure without endpoint labels; the target relies on conditional empirical distributions and selected measurement representations to obtain closed-form task optima.

competitive_landscape.title: Machine learning vortices at the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition
competitive_landscape.difference: Beach et al. use vortex-sensitive learning to identify the BKT transition; the target's energy-distribution optima miss or overestimate that transition, illustrating the value of phase-specific representation bias.

competitive_landscape.title: Identifying topological order through unsupervised machine learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Rodriguez-Nieva and Scheurer use similarity geometry and diffusion maps to find topological order; the target explicitly does not learn input similarity and instead measures changes in selected distributions.

competitive_landscape.title: Divergence of predictive model output as indication of phase transitions
competitive_landscape.difference: Schäfer and Lörch introduce parameter regression and output-divergence peaks; the target derives its conditional-mean optimum and documents spurious and vanishing-peak regimes.

competitive_landscape.title: Unveiling phase transitions with machine learning
competitive_landscape.difference: This work compares learned signatures across phase transitions, whereas the target isolates the exact optimum of three predefined surrogate objectives and their distribution dependence.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised identification of topological order using predictive models
competitive_landscape.difference: Greplova et al. use predictive models to identify topological transitions without known labels; the target derives the idealized predictive output but still depends on measurement representation and distribution overlap.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised phase discovery with deep anomaly detection
competitive_landscape.difference: Kottmann et al. use reconstruction/anomaly structure rather than fixed label or parameter prediction; the target's analytical optima need an explicit empirical probability table and can miss similarity-defined phases.

competitive_landscape.title: Interpretable and unsupervised phase classification
competitive_landscape.difference: Arnold et al. already analytically derive optimal PBM predictions and propose a mean-based interpretable classifier. The target's novelty is therefore extending and unifying the closed-form treatment across SL and LBC and evaluating it broadly, not first deriving PBM optimality.

competitive_landscape.title: Provably efficient machine learning for quantum many-body problems
competitive_landscape.difference: Huang et al. give rigorous prediction guarantees from classical shadows for broad quantum observables; the target mentions shadows as future work but supplies no comparable sample-complexity or large-system guarantee.

competitive_landscape.title: Machine learning discovery of new phases in programmable quantum simulator snapshots
competitive_landscape.difference: Hybrid-CCNN combines unsupervised discovery with interpretable correlation extraction on experimental Rydberg snapshots and finds new phases; the target validates mostly on simulations and does not extract order parameters from its optima.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning phase transitions from regression uncertainty: A new regression-based machine learning approach for automated detection of phases of matter
competitive_landscape.difference: Guo and He use predictive uncertainty rather than only mean parameter error to indicate boundaries. It was submitted four days after the target, so it is not prior art but is a close independent alternative to PBM post-processing.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised Learning of Rydberg Atom Array Phase Diagram with Siamese Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Patel et al. learn pairwise similarity and multiple Rydberg phases without predeclaring them; the target directly tabulates empirical probabilities and focuses on one-dimensional two-region indicators.

competitive_landscape.title: Snake net and balloon force with a neural network for detecting multiple phases
competitive_landscape.difference: Snake net evolves multiple contours and adds a decaying balloon force to map diagrams with three or four phases; the target's one-dimensional formulas require external piecewise decomposition.

competitive_landscape.title: A learning by confusion approach to characterize phase transitions
competitive_landscape.difference: Richter-Laskowska et al. test LBC on continuous and discontinuous transitions and find phase coexistence can degrade it; the target's overlap analysis explains one mechanism but does not validate transition-order classification.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised Interpretable Learning of Phases From Many-Qubit Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: Sadoune et al. learn explicit local and string order parameters from local measurements; the target interprets task optima as distribution changes but does not output characteristic observables.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Learning of Phase Transitions for Quantum Spin Chains from Correlation Aspects
competitive_landscape.difference: Chung et al. use spin-spin correlations and latent clustering to map XY/XXZ diagrams and distinguish transition character. The target uses fixed basis-outcome distributions and does not learn correlation features.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised machine learning for identifying phase transition using two-times clustering
competitive_landscape.difference: Two-times clustering selects representative configurations and creates labels before neural classification; the target assumes the scan-derived labels and analytically solves the resulting conditional task.

competitive_landscape.title: Mapping out phase diagrams with generative classifiers
competitive_landscape.difference: Generative classifiers explicitly model measurement statistics and map multidimensional diagrams with little supervision; the target uses exact empirical tables for three discriminative/regression objectives and can be dominated by density-estimation cost.

competitive_landscape.title: Fast Detection of Phase Transitions with Multi-Task Learning-by-Confusion
competitive_landscape.difference: Multi-task LBC trains one multiclass model instead of K+1 binary models, removing the leading scan multiplicity in practice. The target's analytical LBC still scales quadratically in K and is its slowest closed-form method.

competitive_landscape.title: Machine learning phase transitions: Connections to the Fisher information
competitive_landscape.difference: Arnold et al. prove that several ML indicators lower-bound square-root classical or quantum Fisher information, supplying an information-geometric target and failure explanation beyond the target's qualitative probability-change account.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised machine learning for the detection of exotic phases in skyrmion phase diagrams
competitive_landscape.difference: Gomez Albarracin uses PCA/autoencoder reconstruction error and variance to distinguish multiple skyrmion orderings; the target studies fixed one-dimensional discriminative/regression indicators rather than anomaly geometry.

competitive_landscape.title: ClassiFIM: An Unsupervised Method To Detect Phase Transitions
competitive_landscape.difference: ClassiFIM defines Fisher-information estimation, rigorous distMSE/distMSEPS/distRE metrics, asymptotic correctness conditions, and shared datasets. The target has no common estimand or quantitative cross-method accuracy metric.

competitive_landscape.title: Detecting Quantum and Classical Phase Transitions via Unsupervised Machine Learning of the Fisher Information Metric
competitive_landscape.difference: The companion ClassiFIM study releases ground-truth datasets and quantitatively compares quantum/classical transitions using only single-basis measurements; the target reports mainly curve plots and small exact-distribution cases.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised Machine Learning Phase Classification for Falicov-Kimball Model
competitive_landscape.difference: Frk et al. find PCA outperforms neural predictors and autoencoders on their Falicov-Kimball snapshots and also separates localization regimes. This supports the target's warning that greater model capacity is not uniformly better, through a different similarity-based method.

competitive_landscape.title: Machine learning the Ising transition: A comparison between discriminative and generative approaches
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. compare discriminative and generative Ising classifiers while accounting for data availability, accuracy, and computational resources. It addresses the target's omitted density-generation cost more directly.

competitive_landscape.title: 3-phases Confusion Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Caleca et al. replace binary with ternary confusion for three-phase systems and test Kitaev/Hubbard chains; the target's derivation is binary and delegates multiphase handling to piecewise scans.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning by Confusion: The Phase Diagram of the Holstein Model
competitive_landscape.difference: Issa et al. test multiple imaginary-time-resolved input choices and build a finite-temperature Holstein phase diagram; the target provides the Bayes overlap formula but no comparable strongly correlated full-diagram validation.

competitive_landscape.title: Unsupervised Machine Learning for Experimental Detection of Quantum-Many-Body Phase Transitions
competitive_landscape.difference: Ziv et al. detect MBL and Mott-superfluid collective behavior directly from partial experimental measurements without model-specific priors. The target's MBL validation is a small simulated system with an explicit basis probability table.

competitive_landscape.title: Distance learning from projective measurements as an information-geometric probe of many-body physics
competitive_landscape.difference: Malyshev et al. train one discriminator to estimate f-divergences, cluster phases, connect the infinitesimal limit to Fisher information, and extract critical exponents. The target computes three task-specific indicators but does not learn a reusable distance or universality class.

competitive_landscape.title: Autoencoder-Based Unsupervised Identification of Nonequilibrium Phases in Sheared Binary Colloids
competitive_landscape.difference: Miyahara and Haga combine Fourier preprocessing, an autoencoder, and a Gaussian mixture model to recover three nonequilibrium colloid phases. The target has no heterogeneous spatial nonequilibrium multiphase benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: Representation-Dependent Machine Learning of the Isotropic-Nematic Transition in the Lebwohl-Lasher Model
competitive_landscape.difference: Kaur et al. show PCA and an autoencoder fail on raw rotationally equivalent configurations but succeed after a symmetry-invariant correlation transform. This directly reinforces the target's conditional basis/representation caveat and narrows any representation-agnostic reading.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first unified analytical derivation and numerical use of optimal predictors and phase indicators for supervised learning, learning by confusion, and PBM, replacing neural training with direct probability-based computation and explaining success and failure.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact formulas, six-system study, finite-sample/capacity analysis, and open implementation support a substantive unification. The paper explicitly acknowledges that PBM optimal predictions were already derived in its own 2021 predecessor. Earlier work created all three methods and several unsupervised, interpretable, and similarity-based alternatives. Later work adds generative classifiers, Fisher-information theory, common metrics, experimental snapshots, and learned divergences.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is the explicit Bayes-risk unification of three widely used phase-scan surrogate tasks, together with unusually candid counterexamples showing that exact surrogate optimization can hurt physical boundary detection. The conditional-posterior and conditional-mean mathematics is standard, PBM optimality is prior, and the artifact does not establish a general, representation-agnostic, scalable, or end-to-end optimal phase-discovery algorithm. Current work substantially supersedes its evaluation framework, but not its pedagogically useful closed-form diagnostic.
